text: RF drone detectors such as Chuika, Obriy and ZORKO read analogue FPV video out to about 2.5–4 km, and some show the attacking drone's own camera feed.

observations.subject: analogue FPV video by handheld RF detectors

text: Handheld RF detectors cannot see fibre-optic drones, which emit nothing, and they go blind as Russian drones move to digital video and new bands.
Acoustic sensors can hear fibre-optic drones, but only at 150–450 m, according to the maker's claim for the Zvook NW0.

observations.subject: fibre-optic drones by acoustic sensor (vendor claim)

text: Small counter-drone radars detect fibre-optic drones 'several kilometres' out, but they emit and so can themselves be found.
Against a fibre-optic drone perched on the ground, only eyes on the road work: a drone sweep of the route before a convoy moves.
Trench, backpack and vehicle 'dome' jammers protect a bubble of about 150–300 m around the user.

According to a Ukrainian EW company commander, jamming worked in 2023–2024, but Russian FPVs spread across the bands faster than jammers could follow, and fibre-optic FPVs ended conventional frontline EW at the end of 2024.
RUSI found that jamming causes fratricide, making friendly drone operations 'periodic rather than continuous'.
In early 2025 fibre-optic FPVs had a range of about 10 km, with 'degraded flight performance' and a risk of snagging, according to RUSI.
By late 2025 most fibre-optic FPVs flew 10–25 km, and some Russian types reached about 50 km.
In February 2025 a Ukrainian unit followed a fibre-optic trail back to a Russian drone crew.
By May 2025 the busiest fields were so littered with old fibre that following fibre back to the crew 'doesn't work anymore'.
The waiting drone (zhdun) is a fibre-optic FPV that lands by a road with its motors off and its camera on; the research file judges it the hardest threat.
A waiting drone can wait 12 hours according to one analyst, or days to two weeks on a large battery according to a Ukrainian maker's tests.

observations.subject: waiting drone on a large battery (maker's tests)
observations.note: 'days' taken as a lower bound of 1 day

text: Rubikon saturated 100–300 m road sections with waiting drones to cut the Sudzha supply road in February 2025.

observations.subject: road section saturated with waiting drones

text: Counters to waiting drones are drone sweeps of the route, FPVs or grenades dropped on the perched drone, nets (under which waiting drones can also hide), and speed.
One reporter outran a fibre-optic drone at over 160 km/h.
RUSI counted 1,000–1,500 Russian reconnaissance-drone orbits a day in August 2024, then saw them thinned by radar-cued interceptor drones.

mentions.name: Russian fixed-wing ISR drones (Orlan, Zala, Supercam)

text: According to a Ukrainian volunteer figure, Russian Lancet strikes fell from 180 in August 2024 to 24 in November 2024 as interceptors broke the Orlan/ZALA-to-Lancet chain.
In response to interceptors, Russian scout drones climbed to 4–5 km and gained rear-view cameras.

mentions.name: Russian fixed-wing ISR drones (Orlan, Zala, Supercam)

text: RUSI reported that whenever Ukraine pushed air defence forward, Russia 'successfully found and engaged' it, usually with Iskander ballistic missiles.
A Lancet hit on an IRIS-T TRML-4D radar was filmed in June 2023; the source is secondary and unverified.
In 2023 decoys drew Lancets onto a fake IRIS-T in Kherson and onto a fake Su-25 at Kryvyi Rih.
Russia's Rubikon finds Ukrainian drone operators by radio reconnaissance; one Ukrainian brigade reportedly lost up to 70% of its operators in a week.

observations.subject: Ukrainian brigade's drone operators lost in a week

notes: single relayed claim (Rob Lee via RFE/RL)

text: From June 2025 Ukraine's new drone commander made Russian drone operators the main target, worth 25 points in the e-points system.
Passive direction-finders such as Kvertus Azimuth are offered for finding drone operators, with ranges of about 15 km on the ground and 60 km raised on an aerostat (vendor claims).

Handheld RF detectors (Chuika 3.0/4.0, Obriy, ZORKO, Whoover, Dzyga) give an alarm that gets louder as the drone closes and a histogram per band, and on analogue video they show the attacker's own camera feed.
Chuika detects drones out to about 4 km (reported); Obriy has a typical range of about 2.5 km and up to 5 km (vendor claim).
Handheld RF detectors cannot see fibre-optic drones, bands they do not cover, or autonomous drones with no link, and they detect digital or encrypted video but cannot show it. They do not emit.
A Chuika 4.0 can show Molniya video out to about 3 km.
The Sense 4 detector covers four bands up to 8.2 GHz.
The Zvook NW0 acoustic sensor gives 360° detection on a networked map with AI classification, fibre-optic drones included, at 150–450 m (vendor claim), with nodes spaced 400–600 m apart.
Zvook NW0 acoustic detection is masked by wind, traffic and gunfire, an effect not quantified; the sensor emits only over its data link.
Microphone arrays proposed in early 2025 listen for drone motors; fibre-optic drones are louder because they lift the spool, but 'conventional microphones struggle' beyond about 100 m.
A Kara Dag concept would use an IR laser and camera to see the reflection from fibre, which is hard to see by eye, and the motor heat; it is a proposal not shown fielded, and the laser emits.
In January 2025 a Birds of Magyar mobile counter-drone radar tracked an incoming fibre-optic FPV at 'several kilometres' and cued an interceptor.
TWZ assesses the Birds of Magyar radar as a probable Ku-band type with limited early warning that 'can be detected, triangulated, and targeted'.

cites.quote: can be detected, triangulated, and targeted

text: The Contra-Drone CD-T10 X-band radar (2026) detects FPVs, Shaheds and guided bombs with AI filtering of birds, out to 15 km and 3 km altitude (vendor claim), and is being tested with mobile fire groups.
A networked air-defence radar and live map shows aircraft above a set altitude with speed, height and emitted signals, and is used to cue interceptors against Orlan and ZALA; it misses low fliers.

Eyes and reconnaissance drones can spot a waiting drone in the grass or fibre glinting in the sun, but fibre is 'visible only in direct sunlight or from certain angles', and a camouflaged perched drone or night defeats them.

cites.quote: visible only in direct sunlight or from certain angles

text: In December 2024 Russian forces fielded roadside 'FPV traffic lights' on a mast with three states: 'FPV absent', 'FPV nearby' and 'FPV far away'; they are probably RF-based and so would miss fibre drones unless acoustic (unconfirmed).
Chuika is a passive receiver that scans for analogue video and gives an audible alarm; when it intercepts a feed it shows what the Russian pilot sees, helping the user judge the drone's heading.
A full scan of the Chuika 4.0's bands takes 4–8 seconds.
BlueBird says the Russians 'frequently shift to custom or non-standard frequencies', which forces monthly detector updates.

cites.quote: frequently shift to custom or non-standard frequencies

text: Chuika 4.0 widened its bands to 4.5 GHz for Molniya video and added 6.04–8.8 GHz.

observations.subject: Chuika 4.0 extended band for Molniya video

text: Kara Dag sells detector updates by subscription because 'drone controls and telemetry change weekly'.

cites.quote: drone controls and telemetry change weekly

notes: Kara Dag may be the 15th NGU brigade or a related maker; the text does not say

text: An Azov Corps EW specialist asks for detector coverage of 200 MHz–15 GHz.
A digital drone video feed can be detected but not shown on a cheap detector.
The Molniya's move to digital video in September 2026 threatens to blind the analogue detectors.
A war reporter found in 2025–2026 that soldiers carry several detectors because one may catch a signal that another misses, and that a detector gives a poor sense of distance.
The early Tsukorok detector could not tell friendly from enemy drones.
In Druzhkivka in January 2026 a Molniya feed appeared on a detector when the drone was under 1 km away, 'a couple dozen seconds' from impact.

observations.subject: Molniya feed first shown on detector

text: Near Kostiantynivka in December 2025 dozens of drones were overhead but a detector showed a feed only once, and a fibre-optic 'sleeper' by the road gave no warning at all.
A Chuika 3.0 costs UAH 30,840 (about $690) and has been on sale to civilians since August 2026.
Fedorov said drone detectors 'should be everywhere'.
Detectors can switch a jammer on automatically: 'No threat, no activation'.
Most drones 'sound the same' and share the same radio signatures, so Ukrainian infantry sometimes panic and jam every band or shoot at every drone they see.
Ukrainian drone operators announce their flights to nearby units in Signal group chats to avoid friendly fire.
RUSI notes that jamming and the deconfliction it requires make friendly drone operations 'periodic rather than continuous', and that Ukrainian strikes are timed to planned pauses in friendly jamming.
The Kvertus AD Counter FPV F2 M30 is a static dome jammer covering 420–1050 MHz with a radius of up to 150 m; it runs 24 hours on mains power and sets up in under 30 seconds (vendor figures).

mentions.name: Kvertus AD Counter FPV F2 M30

text: The Kvertus FPV Backpack F3 U jammer for moving infantry covers 850–5900 MHz with a radius of about 150 m, runs 180 minutes and weighs at most 15 kg (vendor figures).
The Kvertus AD G-6+ is a directional jammer gun with a 30° beam, a range of up to 1.5 km and a weight of 6.5 kg (vendor figures).
The Kvertus Kraken F3 vehicle jammer, directional or dome, covers 700–1050 MHz with a radius over 200 m at 30 or 50 W, weighs about 40 kg and costs UAH 350–400k (vendor figures).

observations.subject: Kvertus Kraken F3 (watts)
observations.note: two power options, not a range

text: Dome jammers in general protect 200–300 m, directional jammers reach kilometres, and trench EW weighs 20–50 kg plus a generator.
The 58th Brigade claims its Serval Cube dome jammer 'suppressed every drone' in a staged trial of Mavics and FPVs in 2026; fibre-optic drones were not tested.
In 2023 FPVs flew on a few standard bands, mostly 2.4 GHz and 915 MHz, to which trench EW was tuned.

Ihor Shutyi of the 56th Brigade's EW company recalls that vehicle jammers worked in early 2024, but as Russian control links spread across 750–1050 MHz a vehicle needed one jamming module in spring 2024, 4–5 by summer and 7 by autumn, and ran short of power.

mentions.name: Russian FPV band shift to 720–1020 MHz and mixed bands

text: In Beskrestnov's sector snapshot, 20% of Russian FPVs flew on 400–490 MHz, 30% on 720–1020 MHz and the rest on 2.1–2.3 GHz.
Captured Russian FPV chips cover 300–1100 MHz, so a band can be changed by a firmware update.
Shutyi dates the 'collapse' of conventional frontline EW to the end of 2024, because of fibre-optic drones.
Russian FPV reach grew from about 3 km to 10 km by spring 2025, and the big Ukrainian vehicle EW systems were pulled back from the front.

In April 2025 a 58th Brigade crew drove over a radio FPV hidden on a road in the Kharkiv sector; the soldier believed their stationary EW had kept it from lifting off, and two more jammed drones lay unexploded nearby.
RUSI (early 2025) reports that most vehicles entering the combat zone carry jammers against command links and video, and that EW 'significantly' reduces drone reliability.

Ukrainian ELINT can detect a Molniya by its video, but its control receiver does not transmit, so the control frequency could be anywhere in about 150–2800 MHz, with the operator 30–60 km away amid 'signal chaos', according to Beskrestnov.
An AI variant of the Molniya with no control antenna was first shot down in July 2026; Beskrestnov says its low radar and IR signature may delay detection until it is 'nearly on its target'.
A Ukrainian FPV fitted with a 12-band emission receiver homes on Russian trench EW.

observations.subject: bands on the EW-hunting FPV's emission receiver

text: Russian ELINT satellites map Ukrainian emitters.
Rubikon picks out EW for strikes; per LostArmour, as relayed by RFE/RL, about 15% of its strikes hit radar, communications and EW.

observations.subject: Rubikon strikes on radar, communications and EW

text: A Militarnyi report on a Kvertus demonstration called small-arms fire at FPVs 'ineffective but still common'.
From 2025 shotguns became standard against fibre-optic drones; Business Insider quotes a trainer saying 'EVERY unit is equipped with a shotgun' (known only from a search-engine excerpt).

cites.quote: EVERY unit is equipped with a shotgun

text: By June 2026 the 151st Training Centre warned that 15-inch Russian fibre-optic FPVs carry warheads close to a TM-62 mine, so a detonation at 10–15 m is 'life-threatening' and the safe engagement distance is now at least 40–50 m.

observations.subject: safe engagement distance against 15-inch fibre FPV

text: The 151st Training Centre says a 15-inch fibre FPV is easier to hit with a rifle at 50–100 m, that the issued No. 1–5 shot is too fine for it, and that some mobile fire teams carry only shotguns.
Other ground-level counters to fibre-optic drones in 2025 were heated tungsten wire that snaps fibre, net guns, shotgun teams, daytime and foot logistics, and varied routes.
Gun turrets and lasers against fibre-optic drones were proposed in early 2025 with no fielded effect.
A purported video from March 2026 shows a drone sweeping a road with a laser, perhaps against fibre; it is unverified.
In February 2025 Russia netted about 2 km of road between Bakhmut and Chasiv Yar.
Zaporizhzhia began building anti-drone net tunnels in September 2025.
The Ukrainian MoD's net-tunnel building pace rose from 5 km a day in January 2026 to 12 km a day in February 2026, against a target of 20 km a day.
By mid-2026, 1,066 km of anti-drone net tunnels had been built in Ukraine, with 4,000 km targeted by year's end.
Drones defeat net tunnels by finding the entrance 'or create one'.

cites.quote: find the entrance or create one

text: Anti-drone nets burn and melt, and waiting drones can hide under them.
Large fibre-optic FPVs fly through gaps in the netting.

Armour protection ran from improvised cope cages (mid-2023) to factory cages, then 'turtle' boxes with jammers (April 2024) and an 8 mm steel 'super turtle' (August 2024), each step costing visibility, mobility and gun traverse.
RUSI describes engineers building cages and steel nets over positions near the line of contact.
Buildings block radio FPVs, so troops hide vehicles in barns and warehouses, but fibre-optic FPVs are not blocked and fly through doors, windows and holes in roofs.
A Lancet struck a dummy IRIS-T launcher in Kherson whose camouflage net had 'failed' (reported September 2023).
Metinvest built metal decoys with real heat and radar sources to fool thermal and radar sensors; an M777 replica costs about £800 and goes up in about 30 minutes.
On 30 November 2023 a Lancet, watched by an Orlan-type relay drone, struck a detailed Su-25 decoy at Dolgintsevo, about 45 miles from the front.
The Dolgintsevo base had lost a real MiG-29 and a real Su-25 to Lancets in autumn 2023.
Ukrainian decoys against Lancets are a documented countermeasure, with further material already in the knowledge base.
RUSI (early 2025) reports that building decoy and reserve positions and hides is 'a major task', and that all command posts are buried.
Drone detectors are passive by design, while radars, jammers and drone control links emit.
TWZ warns that commercial counter-drone radars can be triangulated and targeted.
Interceptor teams fly from underground bunkers, with a sapper carrying the drone to a launch point away from the bunker.
Russian bloggers advised their drone crews to move more often, put up false antennas and separate operators from technicians.
RUSI counted 1,000–1,500 Orlan-10 and ZALA orbits a day in August 2024; by 2025 networked radar and electro-optical guidance of interceptors had 'inflicted steady losses' on them.
Ukrainian doctrine targets the ZALA scouts that guide Lancets.
Volunteer Serhii Sternenko's count of Lancet strikes fell from 180 in August 2024 to 24 in November 2024; it is a single partisan count, not an independent series.
The 38th Marine Brigade's interceptor drones (2025) fly at 160 km/h out to 35 km, with up to 1 hour of endurance, and cost $1,600–2,500.
The Russian scout drones targeted by the 38th Marine Brigade's interceptors fly at 60–100 mph at about 1,500 m.

mentions.name: Russian fixed-wing ISR drones (Orlan, Zala, Supercam)

text: Interceptor drones need external target data (position, speed, bearing), usually from radar; finding a camouflaged scout on a small screen is 'like trying to find a needle in a haystack'.

cites.quote: like trying to find a needle in a haystack

text: In the 113th TDF battery and Phoenix's crew loop in Kharkiv (October 2025), radar tracks the scout from launch, a navigator guides the interceptor on a map by matching terrain to its camera, and the pilot makes the final visual acquisition.
An interceptor drone costs about $600, against $30,000–120,000 for the Russian scout it hunts (Kharkiv, October 2025).

mentions.name: Russian fixed-wing ISR drones (Orlan, Zala, Supercam)

text: Interceptor drones struggle at night, and gun batteries had been barred from firing at scouts by day because firing gave their position away.
Russian scout drones climbed to 4–5 km, above MANPADS and guns, and gained rear-view cameras and decoy drones.

mentions.name: Russian fixed-wing ISR drones (Orlan, Zala, Supercam)

text: General Cherry interceptors made 43% of Molniya kills in March 2026.

observations.subject: Molniya kills by General Cherry interceptors

text: RUSI's Ukrainian interlocutors judged Molniya-type powered bombs of low success and 'easily intercepted'.
The first use of a fibre-optic FPV was the Russian KVN, in Kursk Oblast in August 2024.
Ukrainian operators told RUSI that fibre-optic FPVs had a range of about 10 km in early 2025.
An analyst described fibre-optic FPV ranges in early 2025 as about 2 km for small types to about 20 km for large ones.
In late 2025 fibre-optic FPVs typically flew 10–25 km, and some Russian types about 50 km.
In 2026 the price of a 50 km fibre spool rose from about $300 to about $2,500, while a radio FPV costs from about $350.
notes: Silkworm mention is a generic spool reference; the text does not name a spool product

text: Rob Lee estimated in May 2026 that up to 50% of FPVs in some Russian units were fibre-optic.

observations.subject: Russian FPVs on fibre in some units

text: The 15-inch fibre-optic FPV fielded by June 2026 carries a warhead close to a TM-62 anti-tank mine.
A fibre-optic FPV's spool weighs 'several kilograms', making the drone slower and less agile.
RUSI notes fibre-optic FPV range is limited and the fibre can catch on obstacles; a snag 'abruptly' stops a flight.
Frost makes fibre brittle and freezes it on the spool, and the Dronarium centre grounded its fibre-optic drones in January 2026.
One reporter says fibre-optic drones are slow and 'cannot catch cars above about 120 km/h'; this is anecdotal.

cites.quote: cannot catch cars above about 120 km/h

observations.subject: car speed fibre drones cannot catch

text: On about 18 February 2025 Kara Dag Brigade operators south of Vodiane followed 'sunlight-reflecting fibers' to a Russian crew in snow-covered buildings and struck it.
notes: text spells Vodyane; vocab has Vodiane

text: By May 2025 old fibre around Pokrovsk and Chasiv Yar made tracing 'difficult, if not impossible', and many fibres led to abandoned launch sites.
By December 2025 fibre covered roads and fields, and Ukrainian rangers had to decide each time whether a loose line was drone wire or a booby trap, which slowed night missions.
In April 2025 a Birds of Magyar fibre-optic FPV flew through a warehouse door and hit a BMP inside.
The waiting drone is called zhdun, 'the one who waits', and also 'waiter' and 'sleeper'.
Waiting drones perch on the ground, in bushes, under the road surface or on buildings with a view, and sometimes hover low over a field.
Waiting drones are mostly fibre-linked (no RF emission, immune to EW); some are radio-linked, and some carry small solar panels.
Analyst Roy estimates a fibre-linked waiting drone can wait up to 12 hours.
Soldiers say a waiting drone waits 'sometimes a whole day'; TAF tests found an 8,000 mAh battery at about 30% after 3 days and a 15,000 mAh battery at about 30% after 2 weeks.

observations.subject: charge remaining at end of test

text: Analyst Andrew Perpetua describes waiting-drone target zones as 100–300 m road sections saturated with several drones, with group strikes on the front, rear and sides of vehicles, and drones also detonated under vehicles like mines.

observations.subject: road section saturated with waiting drones

text: Ukraine has used radio-linked waiting drones since about summer 2024, and a Russian blogger described the tactic in November 2023.
The waiting-drone tactic was 'a major factor' in cutting the Sudzha supply road in late February 2025.
Waiting drones are 'hard to detect from the air', so units sweep routes with drones before every logistics run.

cites.quote: hard to detect from the air

text: The Khyzhak Patrol Police brigade 'constantly' monitors its zone and kills perched fibre-optic drones with FPVs and bombers (May 2025).
The 5th Assault Brigade destroyed several waiting drones before launch in October 2025.
Gun-armed UGVs reportedly patrol key roads to find waiting drones (March 2026).
The options for killing a waiting drone are to drop a grenade, cut the fibre, or strike the operator; a Ukrainian expert says there is 'practically no effective countermeasure'.

In April 2025 a Russian team watched a Ukrainian rotation vehicle drive in and hid an FPV 'under the road' for the return trip; it went off under the engine guard, and all four soldiers survived with concussions.
Until March 2023 Oryx's confirmed Lancet/Kub hits were mostly on artillery, radars and SAM launchers.
Lancet targets were found by Orlan-10 or Supercam drones.
In June 2023 a social-media video showed a Lancet hitting the TRML-4D radar of an IRIS-T SLM, without which the system cannot fire; the source is secondary, unverified and gives no location.

RUSI (early 2025) reports that Russian reconnaissance density 'has prevented Ukraine from pushing air defences forward'; when Ukraine tried, Russia found and hit them, 'usually with 9M723 ballistic missiles'.

cites.quote: has prevented Ukraine from pushing air defences forward

text: RUSI says Ukrainian short-range air defence that stays back still deters the Russian air force.
Daylight gun fire at Russian scouts was banned for a time because it exposed the battery to fire; the 113th battery said 'it is quite difficult to work from the ground'.

cites.quote: it is quite difficult to work from the ground

text: Counter-drone radars are emitters that can be triangulated.
Ukraine's CD-T10 radar is being fielded with mobile fire groups.

On 12–14 January 2026 Unmanned Systems Forces mid-range drones with warheads over 10 kg hit six Russian air-defence systems (Tor, Tor-M2, Buk-M1, Buk, Strela-10 and a Vityaz 50N6E radar) 46–160 km behind the line.
The Centre for Information Resilience counted a 300% rise in Ukrainian attacks on Russian air defence and EW in March–April 2026, with nearly 80 systems hit.

observations.subject: attacks on Russian air defence and EW

text: In 2022 DJI AeroScope let Russia find Ukrainian drone operators within 'five or six minutes'.

observations.subject: time to locate operator via AeroScope

text: Rubikon was founded on 2 August 2024 and grew to about 5,000 personnel by spring 2026.
Rubikon specialises in EW and radio-signal reconnaissance to locate Ukrainian drones and operators, and since February 2025 has systematically targeted operators flying from far behind the line.
Per LostArmour, as relayed by RFE/RL, more than 25% of Rubikon's strikes hit drones and about 15% hit radar, communications and EW.

observations.subject: Rubikon strikes on radar, communications and EW

text: Rob Lee relays one Ukrainian brigade's report of losing up to 70% of its drone operators in a week to Rubikon.

observations.subject: a Ukrainian brigade's operators lost in a week

text: Fedorov's answer to Rubikon was to move operators back by remote control and, in time, autonomy.

In June 2025 Robert Brovdi, the new Unmanned Systems Forces commander, made Russian drone operators the main target; a killed operator is worth 25 e-points and a wounded one 12, against 12 for a killed soldier.
Ukrainian methods for hunting Russian drone crews include following fibre to the crew, short-range drones on dugouts a few kilometres behind the line, and deep strikes on fibre factories.

mentions.name: strike on the Saransk fibre plant

notes: Saransk not named in this passage; mention is the KB's fibre-plant strike entity

text: Ukrainian radio intelligence once traced a Molniya's signal back to its operators.
RUSI reports that Ukrainian direction-finding is used to cue drone orbits, and that mapping enemy EW decides when and where drones launch.

Kvertus's Aero Azimuth, shown in September 2024, is passive SIGINT on a helium aerostat (Aerobavovna); Kvertus claims a detection range of about 60 km raised against about 15 km for the ground version, and operator triangulation at 15–19 miles. Deployment is unknown.
A Molniya's control receiver does not transmit, so direction-finding finds its video, not its operator, who Beskrestnov says may be 30–60 km away.
Fibre-optic and AI-guided drones give direction-finding nothing to locate.
In the 2023 counteroffensive era, Russia's attacking measures were Orlan/ZALA-cued Lancets on artillery and SAM radars, and analogue FPVs on 2.4 GHz and 915 MHz.
Ukraine's 2023 counters were camouflage nets, decoys with heat and radar sources, trench EW on standard bands, and cope cages.
In 2023 the Lancet's pre-detonating warhead defeated camouflage nets, and decoys worked only until Russian reconnaissance got careful.
In late 2023 to mid-2024 the FPV boom came as Russian bands spread to 750–1050 MHz; Ukraine answered with backpack and vehicle dome jammers of about 150–300 m, turtle armour and handheld detectors.
In the 2023–2024 attrition era the jammer counter failed as modules needed per vehicle rose from 1 to 7 within a year, power ran short, and jamming caused fratricide.
In August 2024–March 2025 Russia flew 1,000–1,500 scout orbits a day, fielded fibre-optic KVN drones and used waiting drones on the Sudzha road.

mentions.name: Russian fixed-wing ISR drones (Orlan, Zala, Supercam)

text: In August 2024–March 2025 Ukraine countered with radar-cued interceptors against scouts (Lancet strikes falling from 180 to 24 a month), mobile radar plus interceptor against fibre drones, and fibre tracing.
In the Kursk–Pokrovsk era conventional EW 'collapsed' at the end of 2024, and counter-drone radars were too few, with a call for one every 2–4 km.
In 2025 Russia flew fibre-optic FPVs at 10–25 km, Rubikon hunted Ukrainian operators and EW, and zhduny lay on logistics roads.
In 2025 Ukraine countered with net tunnels, shotguns, drone sweeps and FPV kills of perched drones, operator hunting rewarded with e-points, and interceptors that forced Russian scouts up to 4–5 km.
In 2025 fibre litter ended tracing, nets were entered or burned, and zhduny hid under nets.

In 2026 Russia used the Molniya on unknown control bands, then with digital video, then as an AI variant with no link, alongside 15-inch fibre-optic FPVs with mine-sized warheads and fibre ranges of about 50 km.

In 2026 Ukraine countered with acoustic networks (Zvook), X-band radar with mobile fire groups, Chuika 4.0's wider bands, interceptors (43% of Molniya kills), more than 1,000 km of netting, and rifles instead of shotguns.
In 2026 analogue detectors went blind to digital video, nothing passive could see an AI Molniya, and shotgun crews died inside the blast radius of large fibre-optic FPVs.
Ukrainian EW company commander Shutyi's account dates the end of conventional frontline EW to fibre-optic drones and the Russian band spread.
Rubikon's hunting of Ukrainian operators and EW in 2025 was a defining Russian measure of the drone-kill-zone era.
RUSI's 2024–2025 picture of scout orbits being thinned by radar-cued interceptors underpins the shift in the Orlan/ZALA-to-Lancet chain.
Fibre tracing back to Russian crews worked in early 2025 before fibre litter ended it.
Waiting drones on the Sudzha road were part of Russia's measures in the Kursk era.
Molniya on unknown control bands made EW against it hard in 2026.
Net tunnels exceeding 1,000 km were part of Ukraine's 2026 counter-drone measures.
Interceptors forced Russian scouts up to 4–5 km in 2025.
